architecture.title: Three telemetry planes of one claw — who writes what, and where it goes
architecture.caption: Agent plane: NAT's IntermediateStepManager publishes IntermediateStep events; exporters (file, Phoenix, OTel collector, Langfuse …) consume them off the hot path, several at once. Policy plane: the OpenShell supervisor and gateway log every egress decision (allow / deny / inspect_for_inference) and OCSF findings, read with `openshell logs` (bounded) and `openshell term`. Harness plane: `nemoclaw <sandbox> logs` and the harness's own gateway log. A sandboxed NAT reaches a collector only through a policy entry (rest, POST /v1/traces); Hermes reaches Langfuse through an OpenShell credential handle, so the sandbox holds placeholders, never keys. (Research tutorial Part 4.)

sequence.title: One Alto Ops request, seen in three planes
sequence.caption: The request makes 2 LLM calls and 1 tool call (measured on this laptop, lab 05-5). In a sandbox each LLM call is a POST to inference.local, so the policy plane should log one inspect_for_inference per LLM span (predicted: 2 — verify on the Spark with `openshell logs alto-ops -n 200 --since 2m --source sandbox | grep -c inspect_for_inference`). The trace export itself is one more egress the policy must allow.

charts.title: What a raw file-exporter trace is made of (lab 05-1)
charts.caption: Event counts in the 454-line trace file of one `nat run` on this Mac (lab 05-1). 94% of the lines are streamed tokens; the spans you care about are START/END pairs. 5 STARTs had no END: the short-lived process exited before the exporter finished writing.

charts.title: Open spans: a short `nat run` vs a long-lived process
charts.caption: Measured on this Mac. NAT 1.9's exporter stop() does not wait for its background writes, so `nat run` lost the tail of its trace (10 of its 15 spans closed); the lab 05-5 run through a long-lived `nat serve` closed all 16.
